questions.prompt: State the derivative definition of \(f'(x)\) using a limit with increment \(h\).
questions.answer:
The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient:
\[
f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}
\]
when this limit exists.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between an average rate of change and an instantaneous rate of change.
questions.answer:
An average rate of change uses a finite interval:
\[
\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}
\]
An instantaneous rate of change is the limiting value of these average rates as the interval shrinks to one point. That limiting rate is the derivative.

questions.prompt: If \(s\) is measured in metres and \(t\) is measured in seconds, what are the units of \(ds/dt\)?
questions.answer:
Derivative units are output units divided by input units. Therefore
\[
\frac{ds}{dt}\quad\text{has units}\quad \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}
\]
This is the unit of velocity.

questions.prompt: Differentiate the constant function \(f(x)=7\).
questions.answer:
A constant function has no change in output as \(x\) changes. Therefore
\[
f'(x)=0
\]

questions.prompt: Differentiate \(f(x)=x\) from first principles.
questions.answer:
Use the definition:
\[
f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{(x+h)-x}{h}
\]
The numerator is \(h\), so
\[
f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}1=1
\]

questions.prompt: Use first principles to differentiate \(f(x)=x^2\).
questions.answer:
Start with the difference quotient:
\[
\frac{(x+h)^2-x^2}{h}
\]
Expand:
\[
\frac{x^2+2xh+h^2-x^2}{h}=\frac{2xh+h^2}{h}=2x+h
\]
Taking \(h\to0\) gives
\[
f'(x)=2x
\]

questions.prompt: Use first principles to differentiate \(f(x)=x^3\).
questions.answer:
The difference quotient is
\[
\frac{(x+h)^3-x^3}{h}
\]
Expand the numerator:
\[
(x+h)^3-x^3=3x^2h+3xh^2+h^3
\]
Then
\[
\frac{(x+h)^3-x^3}{h}=3x^2+3xh+h^2
\]
Taking \(h\to0\),
\[
f'(x)=3x^2
\]

questions.prompt: Differentiate \(f(x)=4x-9\).
questions.answer:
The derivative of \(4x\) is \(4\), and the derivative of the constant \(-9\) is \(0\). Therefore
\[
f'(x)=4
\]

questions.prompt: Find the slope of the tangent to \(y=x^2+1\) at \(x=2\).
questions.answer:
Differentiate:
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=2x
\]
At \(x=2\),
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=4
\]
So the tangent slope is \(4\).

questions.prompt: Find the tangent line to \(y=x^2+1\) at \(x=2\).
questions.answer:
The point on the curve is
\[
y=2^2+1=5
\]
The derivative is \(dy/dx=2x\), so the slope at \(x=2\) is \(4\). Using point-slope form:
\[
y-5=4(x-2)
\]
Thus
\[
y=4x-3
\]

questions.prompt: A particle has position \(s(t)=2t^2-3t+1\). Find its velocity \(v(t)\).
questions.answer:
Velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time:
\[
v(t)=\frac{ds}{dt}
\]
Differentiate term by term:
\[
v(t)=4t-3
\]

questions.prompt: A particle has velocity \(v(t)=5t^2-4\). Find its acceleration \(a(t)\).
questions.answer:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity with respect to time:
\[
a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}
\]
Therefore
\[
a(t)=10t
\]

questions.prompt: For \(f(x)=x^2-6x\), find where \(f\) is increasing and where it is decreasing.
questions.answer:
Differentiate:
\[
f'(x)=2x-6
\]
The derivative is negative when \(2x-6<0\), so \(x<3\). It is positive when \(x>3\). Therefore \(f\) is decreasing for \(x<3\) and increasing for \(x>3\).

questions.prompt: Why is \(f(x)=|x|\) not differentiable at \(x=0\)?
questions.answer: For \(x>0\), \(|x|=x\), so the slope is \(1\). For \(x<0\), \(|x|=-x\), so the slope is \(-1\). The left and right limiting slopes at \(0\) are different, so \(f'(0)\) does not exist.

questions.prompt: Give an example of a function that is continuous at \(0\) but not differentiable at \(0\).
questions.answer:
One example is
\[
f(x)=|x|
\]
It is continuous at \(0\) because \(|x|\to0=f(0)\). It is not differentiable at \(0\) because the left slope is \(-1\) and the right slope is \(1\).

questions.prompt: If a function is differentiable at \(x=a\), what can you say about continuity at \(x=a\)? Is the converse always true?
questions.answer: Differentiability at \(x=a\) implies continuity at \(x=a\). The converse is not always true: \(f(x)=|x|\) is continuous at \(0\), but not differentiable there.

questions.prompt: For \(f(x)=3x^2-5x\), simplify the difference quotient \(\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\).
Use first principles to differentiate \(f(x)=1/x\), for \(x\ne0\).
questions.answer:
Start with
\[
\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}=\frac{\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}}{h}
\]
Combine the fractions:
\[
\frac{\frac{x-(x+h)}{x(x+h)}}{h}=\frac{-h}{x(x+h)h}
\]
For \(h\ne0\), this is
\[
-\frac{1}{x(x+h)}
\]
Taking \(h\to0\),
\[
f'(x)=-\frac{1}{x^2}
\]

questions.prompt: A capacitor charge is modelled by \(Q(t)=Q_0-kt\), where \(Q_0\) and \(k\) are constants. What is \(dQ/dt\), and what does its sign mean?
questions.answer:
Differentiate with respect to \(t\):
\[
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-k
\]
If \(k>0\), then \(dQ/dt<0\), so the charge is decreasing at a constant rate.

questions.prompt: If energy \(E\) is measured in joules and time \(t\) in seconds, what are the units of \(dE/dt\), and what physics quantity does it represent?
questions.answer:
The derivative units are
\[
\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{s}}=\mathrm{W}
\]
So \(dE/dt\) is a rate of energy transfer, which is power.

questions.prompt: Use a derivative to make a local linear approximation to \(f(x)=x^2\) near \(x=3\).
questions.answer:
At \(x=3\),
\[
f(3)=9,\qquad f'(x)=2x,\qquad f'(3)=6
\]
The local linear approximation is
\[
f(x)\approx f(3)+f'(3)(x-3)
\]
So
\[
f(x)\approx 9+6(x-3)
\]
near \(x=3\).

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x)=x|x|\). Is \(f\) differentiable at \(x=0\)?
questions.answer:
For \(x\ge0\), \(f(x)=x^2\). For \(x<0\), \(f(x)=-x^2\). The difference quotient at \(0\) is
\[
\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h}=\frac{h|h|}{h}=|h|
\]
As \(h\to0\), \(|h|\to0\). Therefore \(f'(0)=0\), so \(f\) is differentiable at \(0\).

questions.prompt: For \(f(x)=x^2\), compute the average rate of change from \(x=1\) to \(x=1+h\), then take the limit as \(h\to0\).
questions.answer:
The average rate is
\[
\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}=\frac{(1+h)^2-1}{h}
\]
\[
=\frac{2h+h^2}{h}=2+h
\]
Taking \(h\to0\) gives
\[
f'(1)=2
\]

questions.prompt: A student says that because \(f'(a)=0\), the function must be constant everywhere. Identify the mistake.
questions.answer: The derivative value \(f'(a)=0\) is local information at one point. It says the tangent slope at \(x=a\) is zero, not that the function is constant everywhere. For example, \(f(x)=x^2\) has \(f'(0)=0\), but \(x^2\) is not constant.
